questions.q: What's the core difference between a shared schedule and a report-specific schedule?
options: A shared schedule is its own item that any number of reports/subscriptions can reference; a report-specific schedule is defined inline within just one subscription
A shared schedule can only run once; a report-specific schedule can recur
Report-specific schedules can be paused and resumed, shared schedules cannot
Shared schedules require SharePoint mode; report-specific schedules don't
questions.explain: Both express the same recurrence patterns — the real difference is where the schedule information lives and how many subscriptions can point at it.

questions.q: What operation can only a shared schedule perform, not a report-specific one?
options: Being paused and resumed
Running on a monthly recurrence
Triggering a data-driven subscription
Expiring a cached report
questions.explain: Pause and resume are shared-schedule-only capabilities, useful for halting a batch of scheduled operations during something like a maintenance window.

questions.q: What happens when you delete a shared schedule that multiple subscriptions are using?
options: Reporting Services creates an individual report-specific schedule for each affected item, copying the same date, time, and recurrence pattern
Every subscription that used it is deleted automatically
The subscriptions stop running permanently with no replacement schedule
The shared schedule is automatically recreated the next time it's needed
questions.explain: Reporting Services preserves the existing timing by creating individual schedules for each report/subscription, but from then on you manage each one separately.

questions.q: What actually fires the event that triggers a scheduled subscription?
options: A SQL Server Agent job created when the schedule was saved
The web portal's browser session that created the subscription
The delivery extension polling the report itself
A manual click of Run Now
questions.explain: Creating a schedule creates a corresponding SQL Server Agent job; when that job fires, it adds an event to a queue the Scheduling and Delivery Processor polls.

questions.q: What happens to scheduled operations that should have run while SQL Server Agent was stopped?
options: They're simply lost — they are not queued up to run later once the service restarts
They automatically run in a batch as soon as the service restarts
They're converted into report-specific schedules
They're delayed by exactly one polling interval
questions.explain: The report server doesn't try to recreate report processing jobs that occurred in the past while SQL Server Agent was offline — that time's scheduled operations are gone.
